query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a refractory high-entropy alloy, a small interstitial carbon addition can concurrently increase yield strength and ductility by promoting the formation of a fine, uniformly dispersed carbide phase and reducing the stacking fault energy to enhance nanotwinning.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a single‐phase NbMoTaW or similar RHEA) that typically exhibits high strength at high temperatures but limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low concentration of interstitial carbon into the alloy during melting/processing, followed by a homogenization heat treatment to achieve uniform distribution and controlled nano-precipitation.
generation.conditions: The effect is expected under processing conditions that allow carbon to reside interstitially and form finely dispersed nano-carbides (without coarsening) at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The interstitial carbon leads to the formation of nano-sized carbide precipitates and a moderate lattice distortion that lowers the stacking fault energy, thereby facilitating nanotwin formation during deformation.
generation.mechanism: The finely dispersed carbides act as obstacles to dislocation motion (providing precipitation strengthening) while the induced reduction in stacking fault energy promotes nanotwinning (a deformation mechanism known to enhance ductility despite increased strength). This dual action helps counter the typical strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline alloy, the carbon-doped alloy will show a simultaneous enhancement in yield strength and tensile ductility at room temperature, achieving an improved combination of strength and plasticity.
generation.baseline: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW or similar composition) without any interstitial carbon addition.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected only for optimized low carbon concentrations; excess carbon may lead to coarse, embrittling carbide precipitates and a deterioration in ductility. The effect is also dependent on achieving a uniform dispersion of carbon during processing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in strength and ductility is uncertain and will likely depend on the specific alloy composition, processing parameters, and carbon concentration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one of the baseline refractory HEA and one with a low (optimized) level of interstitial carbon addition. Subject both sets to identical homogenization and thermo-mechanical treatments. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural characterization (using TEM and related techniques) to assess nano-precipitate distribution and twin density.
measurements: Nano-scale carbide precipitate size and distribution (via TEM)
Density and spacing of deformation-induced twins
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility (beyond experimental error) compared to the undoped baseline, or if the expected nano-scale carbide and nanotwinning features are absent, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

The serrated flow behavior [,] is related to the combined effects of dislocation slip, local stress concentration, and martensitic transformation. Bae et al. [] found that the Fe55Co17.5Cr12.5Ni10Mo5 alloy exhibits a perfect combination of strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures. The alloy is composed of an FCC matrix and μ phase precipitates. Mo can act as a strong cemented carbide element in the alloy [], and the precipitates play an essential role in its strengthening mechanism. To enhance the performance of alloys, scholars have introduced various strengthening strategies, such as precipitation strengthening, interstitial solid solution strengthening, grain refinement [], TWIP [] (twinning-induced plasticity) strengthening, TRIP [] (transformation-induced plasticity) strengthening, and heterostructure. The purpose of this study is to systematically investigate the deformation mechanisms and mechanical properties of Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mo-C-based medium-entropy alloys at different temperatures, with a focus on exploring the influence of carbon content on the low-temperature performance of the alloys. Exploring strong and yet ductile materials is paramount for reducing the weight and hence the energy consumption in all fields where mobile structures are used,. However, strength and ductility of current engineering materials are generally conflicting, limiting traditional alloy design strategies. Over the past years, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn great attention as it opens an entirely new realm of compositional opportunities for designing novel materials with exceptional properties,,,,,,,. HEAs were originally proposed to contain multiple principal elements in near-equimolar ratios to stabilize single-phase solid solutions through maximizing configurational entropy,. Recently, motivated by the fact that maximized configurational entropy is not the sole factor determining phase stability of HEAs,,,,, a novel metastable transformation-induced plasticity dual-phase (TRIP-DP) HEA with exceptional strength and ductility has been developed,. Based on this approach, we propose a new class of HEAs which is interstitially alloyed and unifies all known metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material.
